ideas.hypothesis: Firm performance has an inverted-U relationship with the largest shareholder's stake. Exogenous reductions in that stake due to the Chinese split-share structure reform raised ROA and Tobin's Q for firms whose largest shareholder started above roughly 50%, and lowered them for firms starting below roughly 30%.

sources.role: finding: non-monotonic effect of the largest shareholder's stake on governance outcomes (CEO turnover more likely at large or small stakes)
setting/measure: share reform changed the five largest shareholders' holdings and actual controllers in 1011 firms
mechanism: blockholder effects differ by type (state vs legal person) in Chinese listed firms
mechanism: largest shareholder and insider ownership shape cash allocation and market value discounts

ideas.test: Use CSMAR data on Chinese A-share firms, 2003-2009, with each firm's reform completion date and the share-compensation ratio paid to tradable shareholders. Run a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences of ROA and Tobin's Q on the reform-induced drop in the largest shareholder's stake, interacted with pre-reform stake bins. Include firm and year fixed effects and staggered-timing robust estimators.
ideas.disconfirming: The performance effect of the reform-induced stake reduction has the same sign across initial stake levels, or is zero throughout.

ideas.hypothesis: In Chinese listed companies, a higher proportion of state-owned shares weakens the board's monitoring role: independent directors reduce value-destroying diversification only in firms with low state ownership, while frequent board meetings coincide with more diversification in high-state-share firms.

sources.role: mechanism: internal supervision by the board of directors and board of supervisors
mechanism: dominant state shares make boards dependent and enable insider control
method: independent board members as moderators of the investment-opportunity/performance link
finding/measure: board meetings positively and ownership concentration negatively related to diversification

ideas.test: CSMAR panel of A-share firms 2005-2019 with segment reporting. Measure diversification with an entropy index across reported industries and the excess value relative to single-segment peers. Regress on the independent director ratio, board meeting count, state share proportion, and their interactions, with industry-year fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The effect of independent directors on diversification does not vary with state ownership, or it is stronger in high-state-share firms.

ideas.hypothesis: Chinese listed firms whose largest shareholder is state-owned prefer equity over debt financing more strongly than firms controlled by common institutions, because non-tradable controlling stakes made dilution cheap. This equity preference weakened after the split-share reform made controlling shares tradable.

sources.role: finding: Chinese listed firms' financing order (stock, then bank loans, then bonds) and the negative link between floating share ratio and firm value
finding/measure: largest-shareholder type (state vs common institution) affects corporate value
mechanism: choice of listing marketplace and its liquidity as a factor in equity-based transactions

ideas.test: CSMAR financing events (rights issues, SEOs, corporate bonds, new long-term bank loans), 1998-2015. Run a firm-year multinomial logit of financing choice on largest-shareholder type, the post-reform indicator, and their interaction, controlling for size, profitability, leverage, and growth.
ideas.disconfirming: State-controlled firms show no greater equity preference before the reform, or their preference does not change after it.

ideas.hypothesis: Non-debt tax shields crowd out debt more strongly when listed firms are near tax exhaustion. The negative NDTS-leverage relationship is steeper for low-profitability firms, and incumbents hit by profitability shocks (such as telecom liberalization) cut leverage more when their depreciation shields are large.

sources.role: measure/finding: separate debt and non-debt tax shield effects on firm performance
method: partial adjustment model with GMM, including NDTS among target-leverage determinants
finding: mixed profitability-capital structure relationship among listed firms
setting: liberalization as a profitability shock to listed telecom incumbents across East Asian countries

ideas.test: Panel of listed non-financial firms in India, Sri Lanka, and Ghana, about 2000-2015, plus listed telecom incumbents in East Asia around liberalization dates. Estimate a partial-adjustment leverage model by system GMM with NDTS (depreciation/total assets) interacted with profitability, or a low-taxable-income indicator. For incumbents, run a difference-in-differences of leverage change after liberalization by pre-period NDTS.
ideas.disconfirming: The NDTS-leverage slope is no steeper for low-profitability firms, and incumbents with high NDTS do not reduce leverage more after liberalization.

ideas.hypothesis: Among Chinese listed companies, asset tangibility raises long-term debt but not short-term debt, and the collateral effect is weaker for state-controlled firms because soft budget constraints reduce lenders' reliance on collateral.

sources.role: setting/finding: industry (manufacturing vs other) differences in leverage determinants of Shanghai-listed firms
method: system GMM separating total and long-term debt across industrial and consumer sectors
mechanism: country/institutional factors moderate firm-specific determinants such as tangibility
finding: negative tangibility-leverage relation in Saudi listed firms, a contrasting benchmark

ideas.test: CSMAR A-share non-financial firms 2008-2019. Run separate system-GMM regressions for long-term and short-term debt ratios on tangibility, an SOE indicator, tangibility x SOE, and standard controls (size, profitability, growth, NDTS), with industry-year effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Tangibility affects short- and long-term debt alike, or the tangibility x SOE interaction is zero or positive.

ideas.hypothesis: In Chinese listed firms, a larger stake for the largest shareholder raises both leverage and cash dividends together. Controlling shareholders use debt to avoid dilution and dividends to extract cash, so leverage and payouts act as complements rather than substitutes.

sources.role: finding: first-largest shareholder stake positively related to cash dividend payout
mechanism: controlling insiders steer cash allocation inside business groups
measure/setting: leverage determinants of Chinese listed firms by industry
method: regression of capital structure on firm characteristics among listed firms

ideas.test: CSMAR panel 2003-2019. Estimate simultaneous equations (3SLS) for leverage and the dividend payout ratio, with the largest shareholder's stake instrumented by the split-share reform compensation ratio. Test the sign of the cross-equation residual correlation and of the stake coefficient in both equations.
ideas.disconfirming: The largest shareholder's stake lowers leverage, or leverage and payouts act as substitutes (negative conditional association).

ideas.hypothesis: Reductions in the proportion of state-owned shares raise accounting performance (ROA) with a lag, while market valuation (price-to-book) moves at announcement. Accounting and market performance measures therefore diverge around state divestment events.

sources.role: method: before/after comparison of ROA, ROE and price-to-book around a governance event
mechanism: oversized state shareholdings as a core governance problem; reducing state shares proposed as remedy
measure: multiple performance metrics (Tobin's Q, ROA, ROE, P/B, P/E)
finding: state share proportion positively related to firm growth, an opposing prior

ideas.test: Chinese listed firms with state share reductions (secondary sales after lock-up expiry, 2006-2015) matched to non-divesting SOEs by propensity score. Run an event study of abnormal returns and price-to-book at announcement, and a difference-in-differences of ROA over years t-2 to t+3.
ideas.disconfirming: ROA falls or stays flat after state divestment, or market measures move only once ROA changes.

ideas.hypothesis: In both Chinese and Indonesian listed firms, managerial ownership first lowers and then raises the probability of financial distress (alignment, then entrenchment). The entrenchment threshold is lower in Indonesia's family-group-dominated market than in China's state-group-dominated market.

sources.role: mechanism: insider ownership in business groups shapes cash allocation and value discounts in China
method/measure: governance characteristics (managerial ownership, concentration) and a distress definition based on negative net income for IDX firms
setting: capital structure of Chinese listed firms
setting/finding: capital structure determinants of IDX listed firms consistent with trade-off theory

ideas.test: Pool non-financial listed firms from CSMAR and IDX annual reports, 2010-2019. Run a logit of next-year distress (negative net income, or ST designation in China) on managerial ownership and its square, interacted with a country dummy, controlling for leverage, profitability and liquidity. Estimate thresholds with spline regressions.
ideas.disconfirming: The ownership-distress relationship is monotonic in both markets, or the thresholds do not differ.

ideas.hypothesis: Listed firms' leverage responds less to corporate tax-rate changes in countries with shallow corporate bond markets, because limited access to debt restricts how far firms can exploit interest tax shields.

sources.role: mechanism: debt as a tax shield constrained by an underdeveloped corporate debt market (India)
finding: listed firms' reliance on debt and its link with profitability
finding: weak, insignificant tax-shield effects on leverage among Chinese listed SMEs
measure: financial distress definition to capture the cost side of debt

ideas.test: Cross-country panel of listed firms (Worldscope or Compustat Global), 2000-2019, using statutory corporate tax-rate changes as events. Run a difference-in-differences of leverage changes on tax-rate changes interacted with corporate bond market capitalization/GDP (BIS). Check distress incidence as a secondary outcome.
ideas.disconfirming: Leverage responds to tax-rate changes equally regardless of bond market depth.

ideas.hypothesis: Interpreting organizational value as the market value of the firm: because equity issuance by Chinese listed firms carries a lemons signal and debt does not, seasoned equity offerings earn negative abnormal returns and bond issues neutral or positive ones. The gap widens with information asymmetry, so leverage is positively related to firm value.

sources.role: mechanism: game-theoretic signaling model in which stock financing produces a lemons effect and bond financing separates firm types
finding: firm value positively related to the asset-liability ratio and ROA, negatively to the floating share ratio
method: regression framework linking capital structure to firm outcomes

ideas.test: Event study of SEO/rights issue and corporate bond issue announcements by Shanghai and Shenzhen listed firms, 2007-2019, using CSMAR returns. Compare 3-day cumulative abnormal returns by instrument, interacted with information asymmetry proxies (analyst coverage, bid-ask spread).
ideas.disconfirming: Equity and bond announcements earn similar abnormal returns, or the gap does not widen with information asymmetry.
